item.title: Fed's Hammack questions whether Fed policy is tight enough as inflation risks build
item.description:
The remarks lean hawkish and add to the case for further Fed tightening, a backdrop that tends to support the dollar and push short-dated Treasury yields higher. Her view that financial conditions are not restrictive is the more market-relevant line, because it argues against any assumption that the September hike was enough. Fuel costs remain central to the input cost pressures firms are reporting, so oil prices are the variable most likely to shape whether her expectations worry materialises. A firmer rate path is also a headwind for gold, which has tended to fall as hike expectations rise.

---

Still to come:

  • Warsh speaks in Bangkok after hot CPI: is a second Fed hike coming in October?

---

Hammack is less worried about where inflation is today than about Americans starting to expect it, and that distinction could lower her bar for backing another hike.

Summary:

  • Hammack said a worsening of inflation expectations would likely require more aggressive Fed action
  • Warned that an inflationary mindset would make monetary policy’s job much harder
  • Businesses are seeing significant input cost pressures, and lower-income Americans are struggling with inflation
  • Said it is hard to know where the neutral rate sits
  • Said financial conditions do not currently appear restrictive
  • Was speaking at a Goldman Sachs event in New York

Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack warned on Thursday that a deterioration in the public’s inflation expectations would likely require a more forceful response from the central bank. Her remarks add to signs that policymakers are prepared to keep tightening.

Speaking at an event hosted by Goldman Sachs in New York, Hammack said her main concern was the emergence of an inflationary mindset, in which households and businesses come to expect persistent price pressures. If that took hold, she said, it would become much harder for monetary policy to do its job, and the Fed might need to move further than it otherwise would.

Hammack said businesses were reporting substantial pressure from input costs, and that she was hearing more from lower-income Americans who are struggling with inflation. She stressed the value of anecdotal reports from businesses and communities as a guide to the economy, alongside official data.

On the policy stance, Hammack said it is difficult to pin down where the neutral interest rate lies, the level that neither stimulates nor restrains the economy. She added that financial conditions do not currently appear restrictive. That view implies current settings may not be doing enough to bring inflation down.

Her comments come with the Fed already on a hiking path. The central bank raised its target range by a quarter point to 3.75% to 4.00% in September, its first increase in this cycle, and policymakers next meet on 27 and 28 October. Hammack votes on policy this year.

Taken together, the remarks point to a preference for further tightening rather than any pause. Her emphasis on expectations, rather than the current inflation rate alone, matters. It suggests her threshold for supporting another hike could be lower if surveys or business reports show price pressures becoming entrenched. At the same time, she did not commit to the timing of any move.

The comments are likely to reinforce market attention on Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who speaks later in the Asian session, and on upcoming measures of inflation expectations. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: New Zealand manufacturing PMI jumps to 56.5, 15th straight month of expansion
item.description:
The stronger reading is mildly supportive for the New Zealand dollar, adding to evidence that the goods side of the economy is gathering pace into year-end. Firm new orders and production point to near-term resilience, while the return to growth in employment is the detail policymakers are likely to watch most closely. Fuel prices remain the main cost pressure cited by firms, so any further rise in oil prices would squeeze margins and could dent sentiment that is already more negative than the headline suggests. Election uncertainty adds a domestic risk premium to investment decisions.

Newswire cut: New Zealand’s BNZ-BusinessNZ manufacturing PMI jumped to 56.5 in September from 53.3, its 15th straight month of expansion, led by finished stocks and deliveries, as employment also returned to growth despite fuel costs and election uncertainty.

One-line wrap: New Zealand’s factories posted their strongest month since 2021 outside of June, but the firms behind the numbers sound far less cheerful than the index.

Summary:

  • The seasonally adjusted PMI rose 3.2 points to 56.5 in September, above the long-run average of 52.5
  • The sector has now expanded for 15 consecutive months
  • Finished stocks (59.0) and deliveries (58.8) led, with production and new orders both at 57.0
  • Employment was the weakest sub-index at 51.8, but returned to expansion from 50.0
  • Setting aside June’s 60.1, it was the highest reading since 2021
  • 53% of respondent comments were negative, citing fuel prices and election uncertainty

New Zealand’s manufacturing sector expanded at a markedly faster pace in September, with the BNZ-BusinessNZ Performance of Manufacturing Index rising to 56.5 from 53.3 in August. The seasonally adjusted reading sits well above the survey’s long-run average of 52.5. It marks a 15th consecutive month above the 50 level that separates expansion from contraction.

The improvement was broad. Finished stocks led the sub-indices at 59.0, followed by deliveries at 58.8, while production and new orders both climbed strongly to 57.0. Employment was the softest component at 51.8, but it moved back into expansion after sitting at 50.0, the no-change mark, in August.

BusinessNZ Director of Advocacy Catherine Beard welcomed the result. She pointed to the return to growth in employment as a possible sign that manufacturers are becoming more willing to hire. She said strength across new orders, production and finished stocks suggested genuine momentum heading into the final quarter, although respondents were still weighing cost of living pressures.

BNZ Senior Economist Doug Steel said that, setting aside June’s unusually strong reading of 60.1, September’s figure was the highest since 2021. He described it as an impressive outcome given the range of domestic and international headwinds facing the sector.

The upbeat headline did not translate fully into business mood. Just over half of respondents’ comments were negative, with firms continuing to cite fuel prices and uncertainty ahead of the election. Others pointed to seasonal lifts in activity, orders placed ahead of Christmas and firmer demand as reasons for optimism.

That contrast is the key caveat for readers. Strong forward-looking components such as new orders suggest activity should hold up in the near term. However, elevated fuel costs and election uncertainty could weigh on investment and hiring decisions if they persist. Part of September’s lift may also reflect seasonal and pre-Christmas ordering rather than a lasting shift in demand.

The next test will be whether October’s survey confirms the momentum, particularly in employment, which remains the weakest part of the picture.  

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Warsh speaks in Bangkok after hot CPI: is a second Fed hike coming in October?
item.description:
This is the highest-impact appearance of the day. Short-dated Treasuries and the dollar are most exposed to any signal that October is live, after Wednesday’s inflation data lifted two-year yields sharply. Oil is the central variable: fuel costs tied to the Iran war are the main source of the latest inflation jump, so a sustained move in crude feeds directly into Fed hike expectations. A hawkish Warsh would likely add pressure on equities and gold, which slid after the CPI release as yields rose. A guarded performance, sticking to his dislike of forward guidance, would leave the hike debate resting on data.

---

Warsh is the big one today! But not the only one:

  • BOE, Bailey, Bangkok. What could possibly go wrong? Preview and 3 questions for the Governor
  • Preview: Nagel and Klingbeil in Bangkok: three themes as the ECB weighs a December hike
  • Macklem in Bangkok: oil, tariffs and job losses test the Bank of Canada’s hike case

---

Warsh has spent two months arguing inflation will not fix itself, and a hot September CPI hands him the evidence just as markets debate whether the Fed’s second hike comes in October or December.

Summary:

  • Warsh appears in a moderated conversation at the IMF meetings in Bangkok at 03:30 GMT (23:30 ET Thursday)
  • The Fed raised rates by a quarter point to 3.75%-4.00% in September, its first hike since 2023, on a unanimous vote
  • September CPI beat forecasts, with headline and core inflation both rising on higher fuel costs
  • Hiring has slowed sharply, but unemployment remains low and within a narrow range
  • Most Fed officials projected at least one more hike this year; the next meeting is 27-28 October
  • Warsh has said inflation is the bigger concern and opposes giving forward guidance

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh appears in a moderated conversation at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Friday, days after US inflation data strengthened the case for further tightening. The session is scheduled for 03:30 GMT (23:30 US Eastern on Thursday), less than two weeks before the Federal Open Market Committee meets on 27 and 28 October.

The Fed is on a hiking path. In September it raised the federal funds target range by a quarter point to 3.75% to 4.00%, its first increase since 2023, according to the Fed’s published statement. The vote was unanimous. The move reversed the last of three quarter-point cuts delivered in late 2025 and signalled a clear shift in priorities towards inflation.

That shift was driven by prices. Inflation has run above the Fed’s 2% goal for years, and higher fuel costs linked to the Iran war have pushed it further from target. September consumer price data released on Wednesday showed headline inflation rising again and beating forecasts, with core inflation also edging higher. The Fed said in September that inflation remains elevated and that its decision would support a timelier return to target.

The labour market, the other half of the Fed’s dual mandate, is less of a constraint for now. Hiring has slowed markedly in recent months and earlier figures have been revised lower. However, the unemployment rate has stayed within a narrow range and remains low by historical standards.

Warsh has made his priorities clear. In his Jackson Hole speech in August he said inflation was too high and would not return to target on its own, arguing that underlying price pressures had not meaningfully improved. He judged inflation a bigger concern than the jobs market. He also said current rates were not restricting activity given strong investment and consumer spending, and described short-term rates as the Fed’s main tool against inflation. He has also said he opposes giving forward guidance on future meetings.

Other officials have leaned the same way. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack is a voter this year and dissented in favour of a hike in July. She said this week she believes rates need to rise further to restrain demand, while keeping an open mind on the timing.

Markets had leaned towards a hold in October after a weak September jobs report. Wednesday’s inflation data pushed Treasury yields higher as traders added to bets on further tightening. In September, most Fed officials projected at least one more increase by year-end.

Several things are worth watching:

  • October: whether Warsh signals that an October move is live, or keeps to his line against previewing decisions.
  • Energy: how he characterises the fuel-driven rise in inflation, and whether he sees signs of it spreading into wider prices and expectations.
  • Jobs: whether the slowdown in hiring features in his assessment at all.
  • AI investment: given the IMF setting, whether he returns to his argument that strong AI-related investment is one reason current rates are not holding back activity.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Macklem in Bangkok: oil, tariffs and job losses test the Bank of Canada’s hike case
item.description:
The Canadian dollar and short-dated Canada yields are most exposed if Macklem is drawn on policy. With October hike odds already slashed after the jobs data, any hawkish signal would carry more surprise value than a cautious one. Oil cuts both ways for Canada: higher crude supports the terms of trade and the currency, but it is also the main source of above-target inflation, so a sustained move in prices would shift both the inflation debate and the loonie. Tariff headlines remain a second source of volatility.

---

Earlier:

  • Economic and event calendar in Asia Friday, October 16, 2026 - Federal Reserve Chair Warsh speaking
  • BOE, Bailey, Bangkok. What could possibly go wrong? Preview and 3 questions for the Governor
  • Preview: Nagel and Klingbeil in Bangkok: three themes as the ECB weighs a December hike

---

Macklem has argued the Bank can look through an oil shock only until it spreads, and two months of job losses have made markets doubt the spreading starts soon enough to justify an October hike.

Summary:

  • Macklem speaks on an IMF panel on AI and the global economy in Bangkok at 04:15 GMT (00:15 ET)
  • The policy rate is 2.25%, unchanged since a cut in October 2025
  • Headline inflation is above target on gasoline prices, while core measures sit near 2%
  • New US tariffs and back-to-back monthly job losses have weakened the growth outlook
  • Markets have cut the odds of an October hike, but still lean towards a move by December
  • The next decision is 28 October, with September inflation data due on Monday

Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem joins a panel on artificial intelligence and the global economy at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Friday. It comes less than two weeks before the central bank’s 28 October rate decision. The session is scheduled for 04:15 GMT (00:15 US Eastern), according to the Bank’s media advisory. The topic is AI rather than monetary policy, so any comments on rates would most likely come in response to questions.

The policy rate stands at 2.25%, where it has been since a quarter-point cut in October last year, according to the Bank of Canada. Governing Council has held at every decision since. The most recent hold was on 2 September, when it said it was prepared to adjust policy as needed.

Headline inflation is running above the 2% target, pushed up by higher gasoline prices linked to the Middle East conflict and damaged refining capacity. Core measures, however, have stayed close to target, and the Bank has said it sees little sign so far of energy costs spreading into wider prices. In a speech last month, Macklem said the Bank can look through the direct effect of higher oil, but only while those pressures stay contained. He added that it does not want to be too slow to respond if they broaden.

The growth picture complicates the decision. The economy rebounded strongly in the second quarter. However, new US tariffs following the breakdown of Canada-US trade talks have clouded the outlook, and Macklem has warned growth could slow sharply late this year if they persist.

The labour market has also turned. Canada shed jobs in both August and September, and the unemployment rate rose back to where it started the year. That points to continued slack in the economy.

The jobs data shifted expectations. Markets scaled back the odds of an October hike to well below even after the September report, while still leaning towards a move by December. Some economists now expect the Bank to hold this month, though others had been forecasting an increase.

Three questions matter if Macklem is drawn on policy:

  • Inflation risk: whether he still sees energy-driven inflation as the bigger risk, or gives more weight to the weaker jobs market.
  • Tariffs: how he judges the growth hit from US tariffs.
  • October: whether he leaves the door open to a move this month. September inflation data on Monday is the next marker.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Preview: Nagel and Klingbeil in Bangkok: three themes as the ECB weighs a December hike
item.description:
The euro and short-dated Bunds are most sensitive to any steer from Nagel on December. A clear endorsement of a further hike would firm rate support for the single currency. Any nod to French fiscal strain as a reason for caution would point the other way. Oil remains the key driver of the ECB debate: Nagel has called it one of the indicators the Governing Council must now watch, so a sustained easing in crude and gas prices would weaken the case for more tightening. Klingbeil’s comments on German spending matter for Bund supply and longer-dated yields.

---

It's a huge session for central bank speakers today:

  • Economic and event calendar in Asia Friday, October 16, 2026 - Federal Reserve Chair Warsh speaking
  • BOE, Bailey, Bangkok. What could possibly go wrong? Preview and 3 questions for the Governor

---

Nagel is in Bangkok as one of the ECB’s firmer voices on tightening, but questions on French debt could test how far he is willing to push.

Summary:

  • Nagel and Klingbeil hold a joint press conference in Bangkok at 02:30 GMT (22:30 ET Thursday)
  • The ECB raised its deposit rate in June and September, taking it to 2.50%
  • Euro area inflation is well above target and rose again in September on energy costs
  • Nagel says rates are around neutral but has not ruled out mildly restrictive settings
  • Markets and most economists expect a hold on 29 October and a hike in December
  • French bond spreads and Germany’s improving growth outlook are likely press conference themes

Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel holds a joint press conference with German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil in Bangkok on Friday, on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings. It comes less than two weeks before the European Central Bank’s 29 October policy decision. The briefing is scheduled for 02:30 GMT (22:30 US Eastern on Thursday).

The ECB has been on a tightening path since the Iran war pushed energy costs higher. It raised its deposit rate by a quarter point in June and again in September, taking it to 2.50%, according to the ECB’s published key rates. Before that, the rate had been held at 2% for a year.

Euro area inflation is running well above the 2% target and climbed further in September, driven mainly by energy. The ECB’s own September projections show inflation staying above target well into next year, with underlying price pressures still building into early 2027. The labour market has held steady, and wage growth has so far shown little response to the energy shock.

Nagel is one of the Governing Council’s more hawkish voices. He said in late September that rates sit around neutral, but that a move into mildly restrictive territory could not be ruled out if price pressures persist. He has since argued that high uncertainty calls for flexibility rather than inaction, flagging low European gas storage as a particular vulnerability.

Germany offers a brighter backdrop than it has for some time. Nagel has described a gradual recovery supported by foreign orders and public spending on infrastructure and defence. Berlin this month sharply raised its growth forecast for this year.

Markets and most economists expect the ECB to hold in October before a further hike in December. Citigroup has argued that French fiscal strain could make December the last move. French bond spreads over Germany widened earlier this month to their highest in well over a decade.

Three themes are likely to dominate the briefing:

  • December: whether Nagel backs a further hike or leans towards waiting.
  • France: how he answers questions on French debt, having said the ECB’s bond-market backstop is not designed to fix individual countries’ fiscal problems.
  • German fiscal policy: what Klingbeil signals on German spending and borrowing, which feeds directly into Bund supply.++
This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOE, Bailey, Bangkok. What could possibly go wrong? Preview and 3 questions for the Governor
item.description:
Sterling and short-dated gilts are most exposed to Bailey’s remarks, because front-end pricing already assumes a November hike is close to a done deal. If he endorses that view, rate support for the pound stays in place. Any hint of patience, or emphasis on the softer jobs market, could pull hike odds lower and weigh on the currency. Oil remains the swing factor: the Bank’s case for tightening rests on oil and gas prices staying well above pre-war levels, so any easing in Brent would weaken the hawkish argument more than anything Bailey says.

---

Bailey has spent a month telling markets that high energy prices are making a hold harder to justify, and Bangkok is his chance to confirm or cool a November hike they have almost fully priced.

Summary:

  • Bailey appears in conversation at the IIF annual membership meeting in Bangkok at 02:00 GMT (22:00 ET Thursday)
  • Bank Rate is 3.75%, unchanged since a 5-4 vote to cut last December
  • The MPC held 6-3 in September, with three members voting to hike to 4% and Bailey voting to hold
  • Inflation is well above the 2% target and expected to rise further as Iran war energy costs feed through
  • The labour market has softened, which is the main argument for waiting
  • Markets and most economists expect a hike at the 5 November meeting, a week after the 28 October Budget

Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey takes the stage at the Institute of International Finance’s annual membership meeting in Bangkok, held alongside the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, on Friday, with financial markets increasingly convinced that the Bank’s next move will be a rate rise. Bailey is due to appear in conversation with IIF President and Chief Executive Tim Adams at 02:00 GMT (22:00 US Eastern on Thursday), less than three weeks before the Monetary Policy Committee’s 5 November decision.

Bank Rate stands at 3.75%, where it has been since a narrow 5-4 vote delivered a quarter-point cut last December. At its most recent meeting in September, the MPC held the rate by a 6-3 majority, according to the Bank’s published minutes. Bailey was among the six voting to hold, and the other three preferred an immediate increase to 4%.

Inflation is the central problem. Consumer price inflation is running well above the 2% target, as it has for almost all of the past five years. The Bank expects it to climb further into early next year as higher oil, gas and electricity costs linked to the Iran war work through to household bills. The Bank has said those costs have so far had only a limited effect on wider wage and price setting. It has also said that the longer energy prices stay high, the more likely it becomes that Bank Rate will need to rise.

The jobs market offers a partial counterweight. Unemployment has drifted higher and private-sector pay growth has eased, and the slack that implies is a key reason the majority preferred to wait in September.

Bailey’s tone has hardened since that vote. He warned in late September that persistently high energy prices would make it harder to keep rates on hold, adding that the Bank could not wait for complete evidence on inflation expectations. He has since argued that looking through an energy shock only works while expectations stay anchored. Markets have taken the hint: traders price a high probability of a November hike, and a Reuters poll this week found a large majority of economists expect Bank Rate to rise to 4%.

Three questions will shape the reaction:

  • November pricing: whether Bailey endorses it or pushes back, having previously told lawmakers the Bank has no unconditional plan for rates.
  • The Budget: how much weight he gives the 28 October Budget, which lands a week before the decision.
  • The labour market: whether he dwells on its softness, which would suggest the majority is not yet ready to move. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Dow leads US stock rebound. Indices snatch victory from the jaws of defeat.
item.description:
Snatching victory from the jaws of defeat.

The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite closed higher after buyers turned a difficult session for technology shares into a recovery. The Nasdaq 100 could not quite complete the comeback, but its modest decline looked considerably better than the losses earlier in the day.

The Dow industrial average led the large-cap indices higher, with Nike topping its percentage gainers. Small caps also participated, with the Russell 2000 rising 1.38%. The recovery extended beyond the biggest technology names, although pockets of heavy selling remained among semiconductor and AI infrastructure shares.

The closing numbers

  • Dow Industrial Average: +557.06 points, or +1.08%, at 52,183.23.

  • S&P 500: +25.15 points, or +0.33%, at 7,744.09.

  • Nasdaq Composite: +20.16 points, or +0.08%, at 26,713.03.

  • Russell 2000: +37.74 points, or +1.38%, at 2,767.28.

  • Nasdaq 100: −15.22 points, or −0.05%, at 29,935.59.

Those closing changes do not tell the whole story.

At the lows, the S&P was down 49.28 points. The Nasdaq Composite was down 384.02 points, while the Nasdaq 100 was down 542.40 points.

By the close, the S&P had recovered 74.43 points from its low, and the Nasdaq Composite had recovered 404.18 points. The Nasdaq 100 briefly traded up 34.81 points before slipping back below unchanged.

The Dow had a different day. It stayed positive throughout the session, with even its low showing a gain of around 60 points.

The sellers had their shot in the broader indices. They could not keep the downside momentum going.

Nike leads the Dow’s percentage gainers

Nike rose 5.27%, leading a strong group of Dow performers. The gain today was a welcome bounce in what has been a difficult year. Even after closing at $37.16, the shares remain down roughly 42% in 2026, underscoring how much ground buyers still need to recover. The low after earnings on October 1 reached $31.97. That was the lowest level going back to 2013.  Leading the Dow’s percentage gainers gives buyers something to build on, but one strong session does not reverse the broader trend. The next test is whether today’s buying attracts follow-through. The top 5 winners in the Dow today were: 

  • Nike: +5.27%.

  • Salesforce: +4.52%.

  • Home Depot: +4.33%.

  • Sherwin-Williams: +3.83%.

  • UnitedHealth: +2.83%.

That strength helped distinguish the Dow from the more technology-heavy Nasdaq indices.

The Magnificent 7 finish mixed

The biggest technology names did not move together:

  • Microsoft: +1.08%.

  • Alphabet: +0.45%.

  • Amazon: +0.27%.

  • Meta: −0.11%.

  • Apple: −0.28%.

  • Tesla: −1.29%.

  • Nvidia: −1.84%.

Nvidia deserves a closer look. The shares closed at $217.23 after falling to $212.85 earlier in the session. That low briefly took the price below both its 100-day moving average at $214.47 and the 38.2% retracement at $213.15. Buyers responded, pushing the price back above both technical levels.

The stock still finished lower, but the recovery gives traders a defined area to watch. Stay above that support area, and buyers have something to build on. Move back below it and stay below it, and the recovery becomes more vulnerable.

Big winners—and losses that did not disappear

Among the stronger individual performers:

  • Roblox: +7.57%.

  • Macy’s: +6.75%.

  • AppLovin: +6.52%.

  • Intuit: +6.36%.

  • Coinbase: +6.32%.

  • SoFi Technologies: +6.12%.

  • CoreWeave: +5.96%.

  • Lennar: +5.66%.

  • Strategy: +5.62%.

However, the index recovery did not erase the damage everywhere. Several chip, networking and AI infrastructure shares still finished sharply lower:

  • Dell Technologies: −6.92%.

  • Arista Networks: −5.05%.

  • Applied Materials: −3.72%.

  • Vertiv: −3.61%.

  • Cisco: −3.35%.

  • Lam Research: −3.30%.

  • Intel: −2.81%.

CoreWeave’s gain also shows why traders need to judge individual stocks on their own price action. Even within a related group, the results can differ considerably.

Trading lesson: a recovery needs follow-through

A sharp intraday recovery tells us that sellers could not maintain control through the close. That matters. It does not, by itself, confirm that the broader decline is over.

Nvidia provides a practical example. Its moving average and retracement gave traders a support area against which to define risk. Sellers briefly pushed below it, but could not sustain the break.

Now the buyers need to build on that defense.

The same principle applies to the broader market heading into Friday: today’s recovery gives buyers a starting point. Holding the recovery and reclaiming overhead resistance would give them more control. Renewed selling that erases the rebound would weaken their case.

Watch the levels, define the risk, and wait for the next shove.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Crude oil futures settle at $97.97. Highest level since mid- September.
item.description:
The price of crude oil futures settled up to dollars and $0.88 or 3.03% at $97.97. The high price for the day extended to $98.32. The low price was at $93.58.

Fundamentally, U.S. crude inventories fell 8.6 million barrels, compared with expectations for a draw of just 288,000 barrels. That helped to explain WTI’s stronger performance.

In the Middle East:

  • Iran is stepping up pressure on shipping. Reporting published yesterday indicates Iran has changed tactics and increased attacks around the Strait of Hormuz, with operations extending farther into surrounding waters. Iranian officials described an effort to keep oil prices elevated ahead of the U.S. elections. That threatens the recovery in regional exports and keeps shipping and insurance costs high.
  • Saudi Arabia and the Houthis remain in an escalating conflict. Today, Saudi authorities reported intercepting a missile over Medina and a drone over the oil-producing Eastern province. Responsibility for the Medina incident remains disputed. Houthi missiles and drones also struck near the government palace in Aden, killing at least two people. Fighting around the Bab el-Mandeb adds another shipping concern. The Houthi rebels also refused to meet with Saudi Arabia.
  • Transport costs are amplifying the energy shock. Higher freight and insurance expenses make delivered oil more expensive, even when the barrels themselves remain available. Reuters reports sharply higher tanker costs as conflict disrupts routes and vessel availability.

The Middle East is keeping a risk premium in oil, while the inventory surprise provided today’s additional push for WTI. The next question is whether attacks translate into sustained losses of actual exports. item.title: Bitcoin snaps back after failed downside break. Can buyers take the next step?
item.description:
Bitcoin fell to a low of $79,694 today, taking the price below a key swing area between $80,106 and $81,183. That area dates back to August 20 and has been an important reference for traders.

The break below that floor should have opened the door for additional selling pressure. Once broken, the swing area—and particularly its upper boundary at $81,183—should have attracted sellers on a corrective bounce.

However, the sellers could not sustain the momentum.

After reaching the new low, the price snapped back higher, closed back above the top of the swing area, and continued its recovery. Over the last hour, that rebound extended to $82,537.

The sellers had their shot. They missed.

That failure takes some of the bearish pressure off the market and puts the price back within the broader trading range extending toward $87,374. However, returning to the range is one step. Giving buyers more control requires another.

The next test: the 100- and 200-hour moving averages

The next key hurdle comes against the converging 100- and 200-hour moving averages near $82,710.

With the recovery high at $82,537, the price is getting within striking distance of that moving average ceiling. What happens there will help determine whether the rebound can develop into a stronger move higher.

A move above both moving averages would tilt the short-term bias more to the upside. However, the price also needs to stay above them. A brief break followed by a quick reversal would leave the buyers vulnerable to their own failed breakout.

If buyers can clear and hold above that hurdle, the next upside targets come into focus:

  • $84,178: The high for the week.

  • $85,578: The lower boundary of the upper swing area.

  • $87,374: The upper boundary of that swing area and the broader range ceiling.

Those targets give buyers a roadmap, but the moving averages are the first test. They need to get through that door before looking too far up the road.

Staying below the moving averages keeps the battle alive

If the price cannot move above the moving averages, the rebound remains a recovery within the range.

In that scenario, buyers and sellers would continue to battle between the lower support area at $80,106–$81,183 and the moving average ceiling near $82,710, with those averages continuing to move lower.

The $81,183 level becomes an initial reference on a pullback. Staying above it would help show that buyers are defending the reclaimed swing area. Moving back inside that area would weaken the recovery and bring $80,106 back into focus.

A sustained move below $80,106 would put sellers back in a stronger position and raise the risk of a return toward today’s low at $79,694. Below that low, the 38.2% retracement of the move higher from the July low at $76,052 becomes a potential downside target.

The trading lesson: a failed break is a clue. Confirmation is the next step.

When price breaks below an established floor, sellers have an opportunity to take control. Traders look for downside follow-through and for the broken support to become resistance on a rebound.

Today, that did not happen. Bitcoin recovered the broken area and extended higher. Traders who sold the break and remained short were then facing a move against their positions. Buying to cover those shorts can add fuel to the rebound.

However, a failed downside break does not automatically establish an uptrend. It tells us that sellers failed at one important location. Buyers still need to prove they can clear the next resistance level.

That is why the moving averages near $82,710 matter. They provide a reference for judging the recovery:

  • Above and holding: Buyers gain more control, opening the door toward $84,178.

  • Below: The rebound faces a ceiling, keeping the range battle in play.

  • Back below $80,106 and holding: The recovery loses credibility, and downside risk increases again.

The lesson is to watch what price does after a break. The initial move gets your attention. The ability to stay beyond the level—and build momentum—is what gives the move credibility.

For now, the sellers missed their opportunity below the floor. The buyers have the next opportunity against the moving averages.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Atlanta Fed GDPNow holds at 3.6% for Q3 as consumer spending outlook improves
item.description:
The Atlanta Fed GDPNow growth forecast for Q3 remained unchanged as 3.6% after the data dump this morning. In their own words:

The GDPNow model estimate for real GDP growth (seasonally adjusted annual rate) in the third quarter of 2026 is 3.6 percent on October 15, unchanged from October 8 after rounding. After this morning’s retail sales and inventories reports from the US Census Bureau, an increase in the nowcast of third-quarter annualized real personal consumption expenditures growth from 3.4 percent to 3.6 percent was partly offset by a decrease in the nowcast of the contribution of inventory investment to third-quarter GDP growth from 1.96 percentage points to 1.87 percentage points.

The next GDPNow update is Tuesday, October 20. Please see the "Release Dates" tab for a list of upcoming releases.The Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow is a running estimate of U.S. economic growth ahead of the official GDP report.

What GDPNow measures

GDPNow uses incoming economic reports—such as retail sales, trade, construction and inventories—to estimate the components of gross domestic product. It follows a methodology similar to the Bureau of Economic Analysis, which produces the official GDP figures. As new data arrive, the model updates its estimate. Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta

A few distinctions help explain the number:

  • It is a model estimate. GDPNow is not an official forecast of the Atlanta Fed or the Federal Reserve, and economists do not make subjective adjustments to its results.
  • It measures real growth, meaning growth after adjusting for inflation.
  • It uses a seasonally adjusted annual rate. A 3.6% reading describes the pace if that quarter’s growth continued for a full year.
  • It can change as reports arrive. It provides an early guide to the official GDP release, with uncertainty around the eventual result. Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta

What Q1 and Q2 GDP came in at

Using the latest BEA estimates available as of October 15, all on the same real, annualized basis:

  • Q1 2026: +2.5%. Revised higher from +2.1% in the September 30 annual update.
  • Q2 2026: +2.2%. Revised higher from +1.5% in the third estimate released September 30. U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)
  • Q3 2026: +3.6% GDPNow estimate, according to the update you provided. The BEA’s first official Q3 estimate is scheduled for October 29 at 8:30 AM ET. U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)

What stands out in today’s update

The headline stayed unchanged after rounding, but the underlying mix shifted. Expected real consumer spending growth improved from 3.4% to 3.6%, while the expected inventory contribution slipped from 1.96 to 1.87 percentage points.

The consumer upgrade is encouraging. However, inventories are still expected to account for roughly half of the headline growth estimate. That makes the composition worth watching: stronger spending supports the demand story, while a large inventory boost can be less durable if businesses subsequently slow their stockbuilding.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.description:
• Prior was -3186

  • Distillates -2527K vs -1560K exp

WTI crude oil was trading at the highest levels since late September ahead of the release. On the day, it ws up $2.33 to $97.41. Meanwhile, Trump was out this morning in Montana saying the Iran war will end "very soon" and that "oil prices will drop like a rock" which is the same thing he has been saying since it started.  There are no signs of imminent diplomacy. 

Obviously, this report will add to the bullish narrative and that tighter distillate number will add to the tightness in products, though there's some relief with a gasoline build.

Note that the 'expectations' numbers didn't include the private numbers from late yesterday that showed a huge drawdown in US supplies.

  • Crude -11.1mn barrels
  • Gasoline +1.1mn bbls
  • Distillate -1.5mn bbls
  • Cushing +1.8mn bbl

For background, the US Energy Information Administration’s Weekly Petroleum Status Report is the most closely watched snapshot of the American oil market. It’s released Wednesdays at 10:30 am ET, or Thursday when a holiday shortens the week, and covers the week ending the previous Friday.

The headline figure is the weekly change in commercial crude oil inventories, which excludes the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Traders compare it with analyst consensus, and a larger-than-expected build is typically read as bearish for prices while a draw is bullish. The report also tracks stocks at Cushing, Oklahoma, the delivery hub for WTI futures, where levels can have an outsized effect on the front of the curve.

Beyond crude, the report details inventories of gasoline and distillates, which include diesel and heating oil. It also includes refinery utilization, domestic crude production, imports and exports. “Product supplied” serves as a proxy for demand, measuring the volume of fuels moving out of primary storage. SPR levels are reported separately, and changes there reflect government policy rather than market forces.

The data are survey-based and noisy week to week. Swings in imports and exports alone can produce multimillion-barrel builds or draws that reverse the following week. Many analysts focus on multi-week trends, seasonal comparisons and the combined change across crude and products rather than any single number.

The American Petroleum Institute publishes its own private survey on Tuesday afternoons at 4:30 pm ET, giving markets an early read. The two often diverge, but the EIA figures are considered the official benchmark and typically drive the bigger move in crude prices.

item.title: Dow Jones today is showing relative strength
item.description:
Dow Jones futures are showing encouraging technical strength at a time when technology stocks are struggling. A breakout from a descending channel, a successful pullback, and a recovery above important price levels suggest buyers are regaining control. But there may be a bigger story: investors could be rotating toward different parts of the U.S. stock market rather than abandoning equities altogether.

That distinction matters for both short-term traders and longer-term investors.

Four bullish developments on the Dow Jones futures chart

The accompanying four-hour chart of Dow Jones E-mini futures (YM) provides an interesting picture of how market sentiment may be changing.

Let's examine the four numbered observations on my 4h Dow Jones futures (YM1!) chart, because they tell a story that is more useful than simply noticing that prices are rising.

1. The breakout from a descending channel

The first important development was the breakout from a declining price channel that had contained much of the market's weakness since early September.

That channel can also be interpreted as a large bullish flag, a period of downward consolidation following an earlier strong advance.

A bull flag does not guarantee another rally. However, when prices break above the upper boundary, it suggests that selling pressure may be weakening and buyers are attempting to regain control.

2. Buyers stepped in before a perfect retest

The second observation is particularly interesting.

Following the initial breakout, Dow futures pulled back toward the former channel resistance. But they did not quite reach the line before buyers returned.

In other words, the market did not provide a textbook retest.

Some traders might draw the channel slightly differently, placing the boundary higher or lower. That's perfectly reasonable. Technical analysis isn't always about identifying one precise line that everybody must agree on.

The important observation is that buyers were willing to step in before prices returned fully to the former resistance area.

That can be a constructive indication of demand, although it does not eliminate the possibility of another test later.

3. Dow futures reclaim the 20-period exponential moving average

The third development was a recovery above the 20-period exponential moving average (EMA) on the four-hour chart, around the psychologically important 52,000 level.

An EMA tracks average prices while giving greater weight to recent observations.

When prices recover above a previously declining moving average, it can indicate that shorter-term momentum is improving.

The moving average should not be viewed as a guarantee of support. What matters now is whether Dow futures can maintain that recovery during subsequent pullbacks.

4. Price returns inside an earlier trading range

The fourth observation may be especially important.

Looking back at a previous consolidation period, we can identify an area where considerable trading activity occurred.

The lower boundary of that earlier value area extends to approximately 52,361 on the chart.

A value area represents a range where much of the trading volume was concentrated during a selected period. Its lower boundary can sometimes act as an important reference when prices revisit it.

Dow futures have now moved back above that boundary, trading around 52,407 in the supplied October 15 snapshot.

That is encouraging because it means buyers have pushed prices back into a previously established trading range.

However, the current four-hour candle is still developing.

The next test is whether the market can remain above approximately 52,361 rather than merely trade through it temporarily.

A sustained recovery into the previous range would strengthen the bullish interpretation.

The double bottom adds another encouraging signal

There is also a broader pattern worth highlighting.

On October 1 and October 8, Dow futures formed two significant lows near the same price area.

The first reached approximately 50,859, followed by another low around 50,909.

Together, they resemble a double bottom, a technical formation in which the market tests a support region twice before attempting to recover.

The second low was slightly higher than the first.

This does not prove that the broader correction has ended. But combined with the subsequent channel breakout, it adds weight to the possibility that sellers are losing control.

The sequence is constructive: two lows near the same area, a recovery, a channel breakout, a pullback that attracted buyers, and a move back into an earlier trading range.

Why is the Dow improving while technology stocks struggle?

This is where the technical picture connects with a broader development in the U.S. stock market.

On Wednesday, October 14, the Nasdaq Composite declined approximately 1.9%, while the S&P 500 lost 1.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, by contrast, slipped only about 0.1%.

The market was responding partly to a hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation report.

According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, September consumer prices rose 0.6% from the previous month, bringing annual inflation to 3.7%.

That intensified concerns about the possibility of higher interest rates.

Technology shares, particularly semiconductor and AI-related companies, came under considerable pressure.

But not every sector followed them lower.

Healthcare advanced approximately 2.4% and Consumer Staples gained approximately 2.1% during Wednesday's session, based on reported sector performance.

That divergence raises an important question: Are investors becoming less interested in owning stocks, or are they simply becoming more selective?

The evidence increasingly favors at least considering the second explanation.

A rotation toward defensive stocks may be developing

Healthcare and Consumer Staples are often called defensive sectors.

The reason is relatively straightforward.

People still need medicine, medical care, groceries, beverages and household necessities even when economic growth slows.

These businesses may therefore enjoy more stable demand than companies whose customers can easily postpone purchases.

When investors become concerned about inflation, borrowing costs or economic uncertainty, they sometimes reduce exposure to more speculative growth businesses and increase exposure to companies with more predictable earnings.

Our broader sector assessment this week has identified strengthening interest in Healthcare and Consumer Staples, while Technology and Communication Services have been losing momentum.

Financials are another area worth monitoring, although the picture is less consistent. Some banks have reported encouraging results while others have disappointed.

There is an important distinction here:

A rotation away from technology is not necessarily the same thing as a rotation out of the stock market.

And that is potentially relevant to the Dow.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average has exposure to healthcare, financial, industrial and consumer businesses alongside its technology holdings. Its composition differs significantly from the more technology-heavy Nasdaq.

Therefore, the Dow can sometimes demonstrate relative strength when technology shares come under pressure.

Its present technical improvement could be consistent with this changing preference among investors.

Still, this is an emerging interpretation, not definitive proof that a sustained sector rotation has begun.

What should Dow Jones futures traders watch next?

The technical picture is encouraging, but traders still need confirmation.

52,361: The immediate decision area

This is approximately the lower boundary of the earlier trading range.

Remaining above it would suggest that buyers are successfully establishing themselves back inside that range.

A sustained move below it would weaken the immediate breakout interpretation.

52,000: Momentum and psychological support

The 52,000 region is important because it is close to the recently reclaimed four-hour moving average.

A pullback that finds buyers around this area would be consistent with an improving short-term structure.

Repeated failures below it would warrant more caution.

52,612: A nearby upside reference

This was the high reached on October 13.

If buyers establish themselves above the previous value-area boundary, this recent high becomes a useful next reference.

Breaking it would provide additional evidence of improving momentum. Rejection there would suggest that the recovery still faces overhead supply.

51,600 area: A deeper test

The October 14 decline reached approximately 51,602.

A renewed move into that area would raise questions about the resilience of the recovery, particularly if buyers could no longer defend the structure established after the October 8 low.

These are chart reference levels, not automatic orders or guarantees of a particular outcome.

What investors can learn from this developing rotation

For longer-term investors, the story is not simply whether Dow futures can rise another few hundred points.

The more important question is whether U.S. equity-market leadership is becoming broader or simply changing direction.

Consider three possibilities.

A healthy rotation: Technology cools off, but other sectors strengthen. The broad market remains relatively resilient as capital shifts between different types of companies.

A defensive warning: Healthcare and Consumer Staples outperform because investors are becoming increasingly worried about economic conditions. The Dow may hold up initially, but broader selling could eventually spread.

Technology regains leadership: The latest decline creates attractive opportunities, earnings remain supportive, and investors return to AI-related companies. The rotation loses momentum.

To distinguish these scenarios, investors can compare sector performance and examine diversified ETFs such as XLV for Healthcare, XLP for Consumer Staples and XLK for Technology.

Fund inflows, stronger performance relative to the S&P 500 and wider participation among individual stocks would help confirm whether changing leadership is becoming more established.

There is also a useful valuation lesson.

A defensive company is not automatically an attractive investment at any price. Even stable businesses can become expensive when too many investors rush into them.

The takeaway: The Dow may be telling us something beyond the chart

I find the current Dow Jones futures structure encouraging.

The double bottom, channel breakout, early buying on the retest, recovery above the four-hour EMA and return into an earlier value area all suggest that the bullish case is strengthening.

But the bigger picture is equally interesting.

While technology and AI-related shares face selling pressure, other areas of the stock market are attracting attention.

The Dow's relative resilience may be one expression of that change.

For traders, the immediate question is whether YM can sustain its recovery above the 52,361 region and challenge the recent high near 52,612.

For investors, the question extends further: Is the market becoming genuinely healthier through broader participation, or are investors quietly moving toward defensive businesses because they expect more trouble ahead?

The coming sessions should help us distinguish between those possibilities.

And sometimes, understanding where money appears to be moving is just as valuable as knowing whether the overall stock market is rising or falling.

What else is going on in markets?  Cross-asset volatility continues to ripple across global markets following the latest inflation jitters. Earlier in the session, as Eamonn Sheridan at investingLive.com outlined, an extended Treasury rebound pulled 10-year yields down and sent gold climbing toward $40 gains, but broader risk appetite remains fragile.

That defensive posture has spread aggressively into equity markets, where, as Adam Button at investingLive.com warned, credit markets are beginning to reassess leverage as surging bond yields and AI infrastructure debt spark reckoning fears across tech hardware and neoclouds.

From a chartist standpoint, that equity drag is showing up directly at key technical pivots: as Greg Michalowski at investingLive.com detailed, US equities are tumbling through the S&P 500 200-hour moving average and testing the Nasdaq Composite 100-day line, keeping sellers firmly in control of the short-term bias.

Meanwhile, digital assets are absorbing heavy collateral damage as Bitcoin slipped under $81,000, underscoring the structural dynamics Justin Low at investingLive.com recently broke down regarding why thin order-book depth and forced liquidations cause altcoins to crash much harder than Bitcoin during rapid risk-off sweeps.

Market observations reflect the October 15, 2026 chart snapshot and October 14 completed U.S. session. This analysis is educational only, not investment advice. Trading and investing involve risk of loss.

item.title: US stocks have continued their declines today. What next from a technical perspective?
item.description:
In yesterday’s video, I looked at three major US stock indices. Each offered a different view of the market—and a different technical story:

  • S&P 500: The broadest sector representation of the three.

  • Nasdaq Composite: A broader collection of Nasdaq-listed companies, with a heavy technology weighting.

  • Nasdaq 100: A more concentrated index of 100 of the largest nonfinancial companies listed on Nasdaq, with significant technology exposure.

At the time, the S&P was trying to hold support at its 100-hour moving average. The Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100 were trading between their 100- and 200-hour moving averages, giving sellers a modest short-term advantage.

By the close, that advantage had grown. Both Nasdaq indices finished below their 200-hour moving averages. Today, the selling has continued, bringing the next technical levels into play.

Where do the buyers need to make a stand?

  • S&P 500 — 200-hour moving average at 7,706.38: The index has now broken below that level. Stay below, and the sellers retain control of the short-term bias. Buyers need to reclaim the moving average and hold above it to begin repairing the technical damage. The

  • Nasdaq Composite — 100-day moving average at 26,289: The index gapped below its rising trendline and the 38.2% retracement at 26,463, but found support buyers just ahead of its rising 100-day moving average. That gives buyers a level to lean against and some hope. Hold above it, and a recovery toward 26,463 becomes the next test. Break below it and stay below, and another layer of support gives way.

  • Nasdaq 100 — 100-day moving average at 29,626.09: The index has already broken below this longer-term barometer and remains below it. Buyers need to reclaim that moving average and then the broken trendline near 29,700. Until those levels are recovered and held, sellers remain in control.

The trading lesson: Finding support is only the first step

The Nasdaq Composite attracted buyers near its 100-day moving average. That is a starting point, but it does not confirm that the decline is over. Buyers still need to push the price back above broken technical levels to show they are taking back control.

The same principle applies to the S&P and Nasdaq 100. Once support breaks, that level becomes a potential ceiling on a rebound. A recovery that stalls against former support gives sellers another opportunity to lean against a defined level.

Buyers need to hold support, reclaim broken levels, and keep the recovery going. Until then, the pressure remains to the downside.

In the video above, I walk through those technical levels in more detail and outline the next downside targets if the selling continues.

item.title: AUDUSD sellers take control as economic data push the pair down over 1%. What levels matter next?
item.description:
Australia’s September jobs report was weaker than expected, giving the RBA more room to remain patient. For the AUDUSD, the report helped push the price lower. The technical breaks that followed have given sellers more control.

In the video, I look at those breaks, the levels sellers need to stay below, and the next downside targets.

Employment falls, but the details are mixed

The key seasonally adjusted figures showed:

  • Employment fell 39,300, compared with expectations for a 20,000 increase.

  • August’s gain was revised lower to 29,300 from 39,500.

  • Unemployment was 4.7%, above the 4.6% expected. August was revised to 4.7%, leaving September unchanged at the rounded level.

  • Full-time employment rose 34,400, but part-time employment fell 73,700.

  • Participation slipped to 66.8% from 67.0%.

  • Underemployment increased to 6.3% from 6.2%.

  • Hours worked edged up 0.1%.

  • The employment-to-population ratio fell 0.3 percentage points to 63.6%.

The participation decline deserves attention. With fewer people working or actively looking for work, the unemployment rate did not fully reflect the weakness in employment. The lower employment-to-population ratio reinforced that softer picture.

There were offsets. Full-time jobs increased, and hours worked edged higher. The smoother trend figures also showed employment rising 15,700, with unemployment holding at 4.6%.

My read? The report gives the RBA more room to pause, but the details are mixed enough that one weak headline does not settle the policy outlook.

Broken support gives sellers more control

For traders, the economic report provides the catalyst. The technical levels help define the bias and risk.

The move below the 0.69620–0.69778 swing area increased the bearish bias. The subsequent break below another swing area at 0.69056–0.69205 gave sellers another victory. That move was helped by the stronger PPI and retail sales report.  

That lower area is now the nearby risk-defining zone.

Stay below 0.69056–0.69205, and sellers remain in control. Move back into the area, and traders need to be alert to fading downside momentum. Get above 0.69205 and stay above, and the buyers would have a victory of their own.

A recovery would then shift attention toward the broken 38.2% retracement at 0.6950. Buyers would need to reclaim that level to improve the technical picture further.

A technical floor and the midpoint are the next targets

On the downside, the next key support zone comes between 0.68321 and 0.68632.

Within that area sits the 50% midpoint of the move higher from the November 21, 2025 low, at 0.68488.

The combination of the prior floor and the midpoint makes this an important area to watch. Sellers would first need to break below the upper boundary at 0.68632 to open the door toward the midpoint, followed by the lower boundary at 0.68321.

The trading lesson: define what would change your view

A bearish headline can push a currency lower. Sustaining that move requires sellers to defend broken support and push through the next downside targets.

The sellers have taken control. Their job now is to keep the price below the broken swing area and build on that advantage.

Can they keep the momentum going toward 0.68488? Stay below resistance, and that remains the next objective. Reclaim the broken levels, and the bearish picture starts to change.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: US August business inventories +0.4% vs +0.4% expected
item.description:
• Prior was +0.8%
  • Retail inventories ex-autos vs +0.8% prior

For background, the US business inventories report, formally the Manufacturing and Trade Inventories and Sales release, is published monthly by the Census Bureau about six weeks after the reference month ends. It combines inventory and sales data from three sectors: manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers. Together they cover the bulk of goods held in the US economy.

By the time the report is released, much of it is already known. Manufacturing inventories come out earlier in the factory orders report. Advance estimates for wholesale and retail inventories arrive in the Advance Economic Indicators release roughly four weeks after month end. Business inventories completes the picture, adding the final retail figures and the combined total, which is why it rarely moves markets.

The key figures are the monthly change in total inventories and the inventory-to-sales ratio, which measures how many months it would take to sell existing stock at the current pace of sales. A rising ratio can signal weakening demand or deliberate stockpiling. A falling ratio suggests lean shelves and the potential need to restock.

The report’s main value is for GDP tracking. Changes in private inventories are one of the most volatile components of quarterly growth and can swing the headline number by a percentage point or more. Economists use the monthly data, particularly retail inventories excluding autos, to refine their GDP estimates. The figures are in nominal dollars, so periods of rapid goods inflation can inflate inventory values without any change in physical stock.

Inventory swings have taken on added importance in recent years as companies front-ran tariffs, rebuilt supply chains and adjusted to shifting trade policy, creating sharp distortions in the quarterly GDP figures.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: The party continues until the money runs out. Four things have reversed bonds
item.description:
The bond market is calling time out on the AI spending spree.

For a time, no valuations were too high and no spending plans unrealistic. Now it looks like we've arrived at the reckoning as yields on bonds from CoreWeave blow out to 15%.

I have written all year about the unbelievable spending commitments on AI and data centers. It rivals spending on WW2 and is -- by far-- the greatest commitment of private capital to anything. One of the problems is a timing mismatch as the insane demand for chips and power doesn't always aling with the supply chain. That risks big slips in when data centers will come online (and be powered) compared to when the bills come due.

In addition, the rush for borrowing for these projects is competing with the US government, which continues to run deficits at 6% of GDP in good times, flooding the bond market with supply. Moreover, the US trade war is making foreign central banks turn away from the Treasury market and look to alternatives. Finally, the jump in inflation has caused the market to demand higher compensation for all bonds, making the cost of financing all this spending higher.

Of course, none of that is new.

Four things stand out for me:

1. Gavin Baker saying that the spending commitments aren't real

Baker is an AI uber-bull and he's nearly Cathie Wood levels of ridicule as he talks about SpaceX mining asteroids. At the same time, he wrote on the weekend that.

"No one - and I mean literally no one in the AI supply chain - takes the ridiculous $1 trillion of unfunded spending “commitments” from OpenAI and Anthropic even vaguely seriously.... If they could get out of the contracts they signed with OpenAI and Anthropic, they would as open-weight inference is more profitable for them than the below market prices currently being paid by OpenAI and Anthropic."

That's a big sign that much of the spending isn't going to happen and that OpenAI and Anthropic don't really have partners. Moreover, token prices have been falling rapidly lately.

2. CoreWeave, Nebius and Oracle bonds blowing out

This one speaks for itself. The bond market is the smartest market out there and they are calling bulls**t on the ability of neoclouds to make enough money to pay back the huge investments. 

3. Anthropic's numbers

Those were out late yesterday (and maybe leaked out sooner). The company disclosed $16.8 billion in Q3 revenue, which is a jump of 45% q/q but not enough to satisfy the market that it's worth $2 trillion in the upcoming IPO. There is some major fear that the IPO could mark the top.

4. How the Treasury market has reacted this week

The market reaction is often as telling as the news itself. We got hot CPI and PPI numbers in the past two days, yet we saw a big reversal in yields yesterday that's continuing today. US 10-year yields are down to 5.06% from a high of 5.34% earlier this month.

The takeaway there is that despite high inflation, there is a growing demand for safety because the AI trade could be unwinding.  It looks like The Economist called the top.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US initial jobless claim 199K vs 200K estimate
item.description:
• Initial jobless claims: 199,000, up 1,000. Prior revised to 198,000 from 197,000.

  • Initial claims four-week average: 198,500, up 250. Prior revised to 198,250 from 198,000.

  • Continuing claims: 1,710,000 for the week ending October 3, down 4,000. Prior revised to 1,714,000 from 1,716,000.

  • Continuing claims four-week average: 1,708,750, down 1,750. Prior revised to 1,710,500 from 1,711,000.

  • Insured unemployment rate: 1.1%, unchanged.

US initial jobless claims increased modestly to 199,000 in the week ending October 10, according to the Labor Department. The prior week was revised higher by 1,000, but new filings remained below the 200,000 level. Continuing claims edged lower, leaving the overall picture little changed.

The jump in unadjusted claims needs some perspective. Actual filings increased 19,456, or 11.4%, but seasonal factors had anticipated an 11.0% increase. In other words, most of that rise was expected for this time of year. Unadjusted initial claims were also below the 210,777 recorded in the comparable week last year.

Quick analysis: There is little here to suggest layoffs are picking up meaningfully. Initial claims remain low, while both continuing claims and their four-week average moved lower. That gives the Fed little additional reason to ease based on layoffs alone. A resilient labor market would normally support the dollar and yields, although these small weekly changes offer limited fresh direction. The caveat? Low layoffs do not necessarily mean strong hiring.

What this report measures: Initial claims count new applications for unemployment insurance and provide a timely signal of layoffs. Continuing claims track people receiving benefits after their initial filing, with a one-week reporting lag. The headline figures are seasonally adjusted, subject to revision, and best assessed alongside their four-week averages to smooth weekly volatility.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Canada August manufacturing sales +1.5% vs +1.1% expected
item.description:
• Prior was -0.4% (revised to -0.3%)
  • Wholesale trade -1.6% vs -1.5% expected
  • Prior trade +0.3% (revised to +0.4%)

Statistics Canada publishes two monthly reports that track activity in the goods-producing side of the economy: the Monthly Survey of Manufacturing and the Monthly Wholesale Trade Survey. Both arrive first as advance “flash” estimates, roughly three weeks after the reference month ends. Full releases follow a few weeks later with detailed industry and provincial breakdowns.

Manufacturing sales measure the value of goods shipped by Canadian factories. Key industries include petroleum and coal products, food, transportation equipment, primary metals and chemicals. Because the headline is reported in current dollars, swings in commodity prices can distort the picture, particularly through refined petroleum and metals. Markets and economists pay close attention to the constant-dollar, or volume, figure, which strips out price effects and offers a cleaner read on real output. The report also includes inventories, new orders and unfilled orders, giving a sense of where production is headed.

Wholesale trade measures sales by businesses that buy goods and resell them to retailers, other businesses and institutions. It covers sectors such as food and beverages, motor vehicles and parts, machinery and equipment, building materials and personal and household goods. Like manufacturing, it’s watched in both nominal and volume terms, alongside inventories and the inventory-to-sales ratio.

Neither report usually moves the Canadian dollar on its own, but both feed directly into monthly GDP estimates, helping economists refine growth forecasts and the Bank of Canada’s outlook. With the United States the dominant destination for Canadian goods, the data have taken on added importance as a real-time gauge of how trade policy and tariffs are hitting factories and distributors.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.
